framing: Where you cut a document decides what the model can read
paragraphs: A document can survive extraction intact, and then a chunk boundary cuts a deadline away from its condition. Both fragments may still rank well. The answer now depends on a sentence the model never receives.

Chunking pulls in two directions. Small units make sharp search targets and poor reading. Large units carry more context and use up the budget faster. Much of the craft lies in searching with something small and then handing the model something complete.

Our runbook examples compare overlap against splitting on the document's own sections, and then add parent expansion. The counts are small enough to check by hand, so you can see exactly what overlap buys. A pointer to a parent has failures of its own: a stale link, a reader without access, a duplicate, an overflowing budget.

Choose your splitter by measuring, with labeled questions and the final context the model actually gets. Source spans give you stable targets when chunk IDs change. Semantic and late chunking are worth trying once a measured failure explains why the simple structural baseline falls short.
outcomes: Measure how fixed-size windows split rules, and what overlap costs.
Split on document structure, and expand a match to its complete, permitted parent.
Compare splitters on the final context, with stable labels and real token budgets.
question: When a short child ranks well, what has to happen before the condition it lost can support an answer?
